.s("gm_acoustic_guitar_steel").clip(1.5).room(.25).roomsize(1.5)Steel-string acoustic guitar. clip(1.5) lets each strum ring into the next; a small room, as the effects table suggests for acoustic guitar.
.s("gm_glockenspiel").delay(.3).delaytime(.49).delayfeedback(.35)The bell, with an echo every 0.49 s: a dotted eighth at 92 BPM (one beat = 60 ÷ 92 = 0.65 s; × ¾ = 0.49 s), so the echoes fall between the beats.
note(roots).struct("x ~ ~ ~ x ~ ~ x").s("gm_acoustic_bass")Upright bass: the root on beats 1 and 3, plus a short pickup note on the last eighth.
.attack(.5).release(1).lpf(2000).room(.7).roomsize(5).orbit(2)The pad fades in over half a second, stays soft (low-pass at 2000 Hz) and sits in a big hall on its own orbit, so its long reverb doesn't blur the drums.
const keys = chords => note(chords).struct("x ~ ~ x ~ ~ x ~").s("gm_epiano1")Electric piano for the bridge, playing the shapes on steps 1, 4 and 7 (a 3 + 3 + 2 rhythm), so you clearly hear when only the bass changes.
drumsSoft · drumsFullTwo drum kits from the TR-808: soft (kick on 1 and 3, rimshots, off-beat hats) for the verse; full (snare, a kick pickup, eighth hats) for the chorus.
arrange([4, intro], [8, verseA], [8, chorusA], [4, bridgeA], [8, chorusA], [4, outroA])The song: 4 + 8 + 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 36 bars, about 1:34. intro is the guitar alone, so it plays the first 4 verse chords.

How it was made, step by step

Each step is a small piece you can play on its own. The full track above puts them together.

Step 1 · The sus move on one chord

Hold one chord and move only its top note. That's how guitarists use sus chords most of the time: the hand keeps the shape and one finger goes on and off the string.

setcpm(92/4)

// D – Dsus4 – D – Dsus2: only the top note moves (F# → G → F# → E)
note("<[d3,a3,d4,f#4] [d3,a3,d4,g4] [d3,a3,d4,f#4] [d3,a3,d4,e4]>")
  .struct("x ~ x x ~ x x ~")
  .s("gm_acoustic_guitar_steel").clip(1.5).room(.25)
CommandWhat it does
[d3,a3,d4,f#4] → [d3,a3,d4,g4]D to Dsus4: f#4 (the 3rd, +4) goes up to g4 (+5). The other three notes stay.
[d3,a3,d4,e4]Dsus2: the top note goes down to e4 instead. No F♯, so the chord is neither major nor minor.
.struct("x ~ x x ~ x x ~")The strum rhythm: 8 steps per bar, 5 of them played.

Step 2 · Turn the moving note into a melody

Because only one note changes, those notes form a tune of their own. The glockenspiel plays just that note, an octave higher, so the ear follows it.

setcpm(92/4)

const verse = "<[d3,a3,d4,f#4] [d3,a3,d4,g4] [d3,a3,d4,f#4] [d3,a3,d4,e4] [g2,d3,g3,b3] [g2,d3,g3,c4] [a2,e3,a3,d4] [a2,e3,a3,c#4]>"
$: note(verse).struct("x ~ x x ~ x x ~").s("gm_acoustic_guitar_steel").clip(1.5).room(.25).gain(.8)

// the top note of each chord, an octave higher
$: note("<f#5 g5 f#5 e5 b4 c5 d5 c#5>").s("gm_glockenspiel")
  .delay(.3).delaytime(.49).delayfeedback(.35).gain(.45)
CommandWhat it does
[g2,d3,g3,b3] [g2,d3,g3,c4]Bars 5–6: the same move on G. B (the 3rd) goes up to C: G → Gsus4.
[a2,e3,a3,d4] [a2,e3,a3,c#4]Bars 7–8: Asus4 → A. D falls back to C♯ and the tension is released at the end of the phrase.
note("<f#5 g5 f#5 e5 b4 c5 d5 c#5>")The bell: one note per bar, the top note of each guitar chord. Read the chord line and the bell line together to see the link.

Step 3 · Same keys, two names

The name of a sus chord depends on the bass. Keep the keys still and move only the bass, and the chord name changes even though your hands on the keys don't move.

setcpm(92/4)

// the same keys over a different bass note = a different chord name
$: note("<[d4,e4,a4] [d4,e4,a4] [d4,g4,a4] [d4,g4,a4]>").s("gm_epiano1")
$: note("<d2 a1 g1 d2>").s("gm_acoustic_bass")
//          Dsus2 Asus4 Gsus2 Dsus4
CommandWhat it does
[d4,e4,a4] over d2D E A counted from D: 0, +2, +7 = Dsus2.
[d4,e4,a4] over a1The same keys counted from A: A D E = 0, +5, +7 = Asus4.
[d4,g4,a4] over g1G A D = 0, +2, +7 = Gsus2.
[d4,g4,a4] over d2D G A = 0, +5, +7 = Dsus4. It wants to go to D, which is where the chorus starts.

Step 4 · The strongest pull: 7sus4 → 7 → home

At the end of the chorus, A7sus4 → A7 → D does the "lean and resolve" twice in a row. The sus note D falls to C♯ (A7), and C♯ then pulls up to D, the home note of the key.

setcpm(92/4)

$: note("<[a2,e3,g3,d4] [a2,e3,g3,c#4] [d3,a3,d4,f#4] [d3,a3,d4,f#4]>").s("piano")
$: note("<d5 c#5 d5 ~>").s("gm_glockenspiel").gain(.5)
CommandWhat it does
[a2,e3,g3,d4]A7sus4 = A7 with D in place of C♯: recipe 0 5 7 10. In Strudel's chord() it's A7sus.
[a2,e3,g3,c#4]A7: D falls to C♯. The G in it also wants to fall, to F♯.
[d3,a3,d4,f#4]D: both wishes come true. C♯ goes up to D and G goes down to F♯. Home.
note("<d5 c#5 d5 ~>")The bell plays the line D → C♯ → D, then rests (~) for the last bar.

Make it your own

  • Use chord names instead of notes: chord("<D Dsus D D2>").voicing().s("piano"). Remember: in Strudel sus4 is sus and sus2 is 2.
  • Change the key: the same move works on any major chord. On A: [a2,e3,a3,c#4] → [a2,e3,a3,d4] → [a2,e3,a3,b3] (A, Asus4, Asus2). Check the notes in the table of all 12 sus chords.
  • Hear it without sus: replace every sus chord in verse with the plain chord (g4 → f#4, e4 → f#4). The song still works, but it sits still.
